issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. vignette:
The robbery happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just after the dinner rush had ended at the hotel. Arthur, then sixty-four, was walking through the back parking lot toward his car, a routine he had performed thousands of times over his thirty-seven years as manager. He smelled the alcohol before he saw the man—a sour, sweet stench of cheap whiskey that seemed to fill the whole carport. Then the voice came, low and close: "Give me your wallet, old man." Arthur turned and saw a face inches from his own, the man's eyes glassy and unfocused, his hand jammed into his jacket pocket in a way that suggested a weapon. Arthur handed over his wallet without a word, and the man shoved him hard against the car door before disappearing into the dark. The police arrived, took a report, and found nothing. Arthur drove home in a daze, his hands shaking on the wheel, and told his wife he was fine.

He was not fine. In the weeks that followed, Arthur found himself scanning every guest who walked into the lobby, watching their hands, studying their eyes. He had always been a gregarious man, the kind of manager who remembered names and asked about grandchildren, but now he caught himself pulling back from conversations, his attention fixed on exits and sightlines. When a guest leaned in too quickly to ask a question, Arthur flinched. When a maintenance worker clattered a metal cart in the hallway, Arthur's heart seized in his chest before he could stop it. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, that people could not be trusted, and that he had been permanently humiliated by what happened—a grown man, a manager, frozen and compliant while a drunk took everything from him. These beliefs pressed on him constantly, and because he was certain that danger lurked behind every ordinary moment, he remained watchful and on guard even inside his own home, sitting at his own kitchen table with his wife across from him, still scanning the windows.

Arthur's hypervigilance made the triggers worse. Because he was always watching, he noticed things he might once have missed: a guest lingering too long in the corridor, a delivery driver who wouldn't meet his eyes, the faint smell of alcohol on a patron's breath in the bar. Each of these became a moment of alarm. The smell was the worst—a single whiff of whiskey or beer and Arthur's throat would tighten, his palms would go slick, and he would find himself backing away from the person without quite knowing he was doing it. Loud noises, too, had become unbearable: a dropped tray in the kitchen, a door slamming in the hallway, a car backfiring outside. Each sound sent a jolt through him, and he would freeze, waiting for the threat to materialize. He also reacted with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly—a colleague clapping him on the shoulder, his wife reaching for his hand in the dark—and he knew his flinch was visible, that people were starting to notice.

Over the months, Arthur's avoidance became a quiet, steady erosion of his life. He stopped walking through the back parking lot after dark, then stopped parking there at all, using the valet entrance instead. He began delegating evening shifts to his assistant manager, claiming fatigue. At home, he moved his armchair so that it faced the front door, and he checked the locks three times before bed. His wife asked him why he seemed so distant, and he told her he was just tired from work. He did not tell her that he had started to feel like a stranger in his own life, that the humiliation had calcified into something heavier, a conviction that he had failed not only himself but everyone who depended on him.

What finally brought Arthur to seek help was a small, ordinary moment. A guest at the front desk, a woman in her sixties, reached into her purse for her credit card, and for a split second Arthur saw the motion as a hand reaching into a jacket pocket. He stepped backward so fast that he knocked over a potted plant. The guest looked at him with concern. His assistant manager, a young woman named Carla, put a hand on his arm and asked if he was okay. Arthur pulled away so sharply that she withdrew her hand and said nothing more. That night, sitting in his armchair facing the door, Arthur realized he could not keep living this way—watchful, ashamed, startled by every sound and every touch, unable to trust the world he had spent a lifetime navigating. He made an appointment with a therapist the next morning, uncertain whether anything could help, but certain that something had to change.
